items.title: Jerry Jerome interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: years before when I was with Reiser I had sat in with Basie in Kansas City in 1937 when he had the little six, seven piece band.

ctx.x: Oh, it was so important, Monk, that when you think of a town like New York with WMCA, WNEW, small stations, local, that covered only a bit of Connecticut, a bit of Jersey and New York basically, had ten piece orchestras for staff. And there were 300 men employed at NBC, ABC and CBS. Every theater had a pit band. Music was flourishing. It was it. It was entertainment. Oh I loved that job. You know I got fat and furious. But again it was, while I played some jazz, it was all marked according to time because we had…

called “Jive at Five.” And he got the outstanding players that came into the city with their bands like Tommy Dorsey or Goodman or Shaw, and they’d be thrilled to come out and do the show for nothing, because he plugged the records. And he was the most important disc jockey, not only in New York but probably all over the country. items.title: 68642_Jo Jones oral history interview
items.q: Jerry Jerome was playing right across the street from the Reno, directly across the street. He heard that band; he knew that band.

ctx.x: I worked last week with a drummer that I consider a very great drummer and a milestone in jazz history and he knows you very well and loves you dearly, and I'm sure you love him. But I'd like for you just to say something about him. His name is Cliff Leeman. He said he was around Kansas City when you were around there.

Cliff Leeman came from Dan Murphy's Musical Skippers all the way from Portland, Oregon. Cliff Leeman quit the band in Kansas City and he was a sub-drummer with the jump-up band that Basie had. Nobody ever heard that band to speak of but people like - when Woody Herman came in with Isham Jones, Jerry Jerome was playing across the street but Cliff Leeman was in the place before I'd get there because I was babysitting.
